title: Boundaries & Difficult Conversations
description: First unit: Preferences, requests and boundaries. Work through real situations, competing explanations and practical choices.

lessons.title: What is really happening?
lessons.teach: Rae dislikes receiving work calls after 7 pm. Kit is a colleague whose project sometimes runs late.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Listen closely to what each person says and what still remains uncertain.
nodes.conceptId: boundaries-module-01:Assertiveness, behavioural boundaries and shared problem-solving

nodes.scenario: Rae dislikes receiving work calls after 7 pm. Kit is a colleague whose project sometimes runs late.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Could you stop calling me after seven?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Sometimes the reports don't come through until eight.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I need my evenings to be uninterrupted.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I can't promise never to call if something urgent happens.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I understand that. I can answer during my working hours, or we can agree on an emergency route.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So you're not saying I can never contact you?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I'm saying I won't routinely respond outside my hours. We need a plan for genuine emergencies.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: All right. Let's define what actually counts as urgent.

options.feedback: Possible explanations need not be equally supported. We should compare their fit with the actual evidence.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
A partner says, 'My boundary is that you're not allowed to talk to any of your old friends.' The other partner wants to distinguish a request from control.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

nodes.title: Apply the method elsewhere

nodes.explanation: Transfer the reasoning method rather than an explanation from the first case. Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Rae names a limit on her own availability and proposes a way to meet legitimate work needs. This differs from prescribing what another adult is allowed to do.

Calling something a boundary does not automatically make the request fair; whose choices are being governed and what happens when people disagree matter.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
